\begin{proof}
Let $G$ be a nonabelian group of order $pq$, where $p>q$ are primes and $q\mid p-1$. By Sylow's theorems, the Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ is unique and hence normal, while a Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$ has order $q$. Thus $P=\langle b\rangle\cong C_p$ and $Q=\langle a\rangle\cong C_q$.

Conjugation gives a homomorphism $Q\to\operatorname{Aut}(P)\cong C_{p-1}$. Since $G$ is nonabelian, this homomorphism is nontrivial. Its image therefore has order $q$, and $\operatorname{Aut}(P)$ has a unique subgroup of order $q$. If $k$ generates $\operatorname{Aut}(P)$, then, after choosing $a$ suitably, the action has the form
\[
aba^{-1}=b^{k^{(p-1)/q}}.
\]
Any other choice of generator of the same image replaces $a$ by $a^l$ for some $1\le l\le q-1$; hence all nonabelian groups have the presentation
\[
\langle a,b\mid a^q=b^p=1,\ aba^{-1}=b^{k^{(p-1)/q}}\rangle
\]
up to isomorphism. More explicitly, if $G'$ has action $cdc^{-1}=d^{k^{l(p-1)/q}}$, define $\phi:G'\to G$ by $\phi(c)=a^l$ and $\phi(d)=b$. The defining relation is preserved, so $\phi$ is a homomorphism. Both groups have order $pq$, and $\phi(c),\phi(d)$ generate $G$; hence $\phi$ is surjective and therefore an isomorphism. Thus any two nonabelian groups of order $pq$ are isomorphic.
\end{proof}

\[
aba^{-1}=b^{k^{l(p-1)/q}},\qquad 1\le l\le q-1.
\]

\[
aba^{-1}=b^{k^{(p-1)/q}},
\qquad cdc^{-1}=d^{k^{l(p-1)/q}}.
\]

\[
\phi(c)\phi(d)\phi(c)^{-1}=a^lba^{-l}=b^{k^{l(p-1)/q}}=\phi(d)^{k^{l(p-1)/q}},
\]
so all defining relations of $G'$ are preserved. Therefore $\phi$ is a homomorphism. Its image contains $a^l$, which generates $\langle a\rangle$, and $b$, which generates $P$, so $\phi$ is surjective. Since $|G'|=|G|=pq$, $\phi$ is an isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $G$ and $G'$ be nonabelian groups of order $pq$, with $p>q$ and $q\mid p-1$. We prove that both are isomorphic to the same semidirect product.

For either group, Sylow's theorems give a unique normal Sylow $p$-subgroup $P\cong C_p$ and a Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q\cong C_q$. Thus the group is a semidirect product $C_p\rtimes C_q$. Conjugation defines a homomorphism
\[
Q\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(P)\cong C_{p-1}.
\]
The action is nontrivial, since a trivial action would make the semidirect product $C_p\times C_q$ cyclic and hence abelian. Therefore its image is the unique subgroup of order $q$ in $C_{p-1}$.

Fix a generator $k$ of $C_{p-1}$. If $P=\langle b\rangle$ and $Q=\langle a\rangle$, then for some $l\in\{1,\ldots,q-1\}$,
\[
aba^{-1}=b^{k^{l(p-1)/q}}.
\]
Changing the generator of $Q$ from $a$ to $a^l$ changes the exponent to $k^{(p-1)/q}$. Hence every nonabelian group of order $pq$ is isomorphic to the fixed semidirect product
\[
C_p\rtimes C_q,
\quad	ext{where a generator of }C_q	ext{ acts on }C_p	ext{ by }b\mapsto b^{k^{(p-1)/q}}.
\]

Equivalently, if $G'$ has generators $c,d$ satisfying
\[
cdc^{-1}=d^{k^{l(p-1)/q}},
\]
then $c\mapsto a^l$ and $d\mapsto b$ preserves the presentation relations and defines a homomorphism $G'\to G$. The images generate $G$, so the homomorphism is surjective; equal finite orders then make it an isomorphism. Thus $G\cong G'$, as required.
\end{proof}
